note: Name pronunciations for UK families. Each entry lists pronunciations most-common-first. ipa: British IPA; respell: house respelling (stressed syllable in CAPITALS, see js/pronounce/respell.js); say: plain text tuned so ordinary text-to-speech voices say it right. Authored and cross-checked by two independent passes, adjudicated, and machine-checked with tools/check-lexicon.mjs (espeak-ng). Still needs native-speaker review before launch.

entries.name: Aaliyah
entries.note: Stress on LEE, as the singer Aaliyah said it. Some Arabic-speaking families stress the first syllable: AH-li-yuh.

entries.name: Aanya
entries.note: The double a means a long 'ah'.

entries.name: Aarav
entries.note: Means 'peaceful'.

entries.name: Abdi
entries.note: Means 'servant (of God)'.

entries.name: Adaeze
entries.note: Means 'princess' (king's daughter). All four vowels are said.

entries.name: Aditi
entries.note: In Hindi the first a is short, like the u in 'cup'.

entries.name: Advik
entries.note: Means 'unique'.

entries.name: Ahmed
entries.note: In Arabic the h is breathy, but in the UK it is usually almost silent.

entries.name: Ailbhe
entries.note: bh = v.

entries.name: Ailsa
entries.note: After Ailsa Craig.

entries.name: Aisling
entries.note: Not 'AYZ-ling'. The spelling Aislinn is sometimes said differently.

entries.name: Akosua
entries.note: The Akan day name for a girl born on a Sunday.

entries.name: Alasdair
entries.note: Scottish speakers pronounce the final r.

entries.name: Alexandru
entries.note: The Romanian form of Alexander.

entries.name: Ali
entries.note: Muslim families stress the second syllable (a-LEE). As an English name (short for Alison or Alice) it is AL-ee.

entries.name: Ama
entries.note: The Akan day name for a girl born on a Saturday. Both vowels are a full 'ah'.

entries.name: Amani
entries.note: Means 'peace'.

entries.name: Amira
entries.note: Means 'princess'.

entries.name: Anaïs
entries.note: Three syllables with the stress on the end; the s is pronounced.

entries.name: Ananya
entries.note: Means 'unique'.

entries.name: Anaya
entries.note: Used by Hindu and Muslim families. The stress is on the middle 'nah'.

entries.name: Andrea
entries.note: In Italy Andrea is a boy's name (an-DRAY-uh); in the UK it is usually a girl's name.

entries.name: Andrei
entries.note: The Romanian and Eastern European form of Andrew.

entries.name: Anja
entries.note: The j sounds like y.

entries.name: Anouk
entries.note: Stress on NOOK. Dutch families start with a long 'ah'.

entries.name: Antoni
entries.note: The Polish form of Anthony. The stress is on the second syllable.

entries.name: Aodhán
entries.note: Irish original of Aidan. Some Irish speakers drop the d (AY-awn).

entries.name: Aoi
entries.note: Means 'blue' or 'hollyhock'. In Japanese it has three even beats: ah-oh-ee.

entries.name: Aoibh
entries.note: Rhymes with 'Eve'.

entries.name: Aoibheann
entries.note: bh = v.

entries.name: Aoibhinn
entries.note: bh = v.

entries.name: Aoife
entries.note: ao = 'ee'.

entries.name: Ardit
entries.note: Means 'golden day'.

entries.name: Ariel
entries.note: Means 'lion of God'. In Israel it is mostly a boy's name.

entries.name: Arjun
entries.note: The hero of the Mahabharata. In Hindi and Punjabi the first a is short, closer to UR-juun.

entries.name: Arnab
entries.note: Means 'ocean'. Bengali families say OR-nob. Hindi speakers may say AR-nuhb.

entries.name: Arnav
entries.note: Means 'ocean'. In Hindi the first vowel is shorter (closer to UR-nuhv).

entries.name: Arya
entries.note: Usually two syllables (AR-yuh); some families say it like Aria.

entries.name: Aurelia
entries.note: Italian and Spanish families say ow-RAY-lee-uh.

entries.name: Ayaan
entries.note: Used as a boy's name in South Asian Muslim and Hindu families (meaning 'gift of God') and as a girl's name in Somali families (meaning 'luck'). All use the long 'ahn' at the end.

entries.name: Ayesha
entries.note: Same name as Aisha; the spelling Ayesha is most used by Pakistani, Indian and Bangladeshi families.

entries.name: Ayla
entries.note: Families are split; Turkish and Hebrew speakers say EYE-luh.

entries.name: Ayo
entries.note: Means 'joy'. Most UK families say EYE-oh; in Yoruba it is closer to AH-yaw.

entries.name: Ayomide
entries.note: Means 'my joy has come'.

entries.name: Beatrice
entries.note: Italian families say bay-uh-TREE-chay.

entries.name: Besa
entries.note: Means 'faith' or 'a promise kept'.

entries.name: Bjørn
entries.note: One syllable; the B and J run together as 'by'. Scandinavian families say it closer to BYURN.

entries.name: Bláthnaid
entries.note: th is silent.

entries.name: Cai
entries.note: Welsh form of Kay. Sounds the same as Kai.

entries.name: Caio
entries.note: Two syllables. Portuguese and Brazilian families end it with an oo sound.

entries.name: Caoilfhionn
entries.note: fh is silent. Often anglicised as Keelin.

entries.name: Caoimhe
entries.note: mh = v. Some Connacht speakers say KEE-wuh.

entries.name: Caoimhín
entries.note: Irish form of Kevin; mh = v.

entries.name: Cathal
entries.note: th sounds like h; not 'KATH-ul'.

entries.name: Catriona
entries.note: The Irish spelling Caitríona is often said kuh-TREE-uh-nuh.

entries.name: Cerys
entries.note: C is always hard.

entries.name: Chiamaka
entries.note: Means 'God is beautiful'. Say every vowel fully: the second syllable is 'ah', not 'uh'.

entries.name: Chiara
entries.note: Ch sounds like k. Italian families run the first two sounds together (KYAH-ruh).

entries.name: Chidi
entries.note: Means 'God exists'.

entries.name: Chidinma
entries.note: Means 'God is good'.

entries.name: Chinonso
entries.note: Means 'God is near'.

entries.name: Chioma
entries.note: Means 'good God'. The o is open, like the o in 'hot'. Often said chee-OH-mah in English.

entries.name: Chisom
entries.note: Means 'God is with me'.

entries.name: Chloe
entries.note: The ch sounds like k; two syllables.

entries.name: Cian
entries.note: C is always hard.

entries.name: Ciara
entries.note: C is always hard. The Irish pronunciation rhymes with 'Keira'.

entries.name: Cillian
entries.note: C is always hard.

entries.name: Ciorstaidh
entries.note: Gaelic form of Kirsty. Gaelic-speaking families may use a more Gaelic pronunciation, so check.

entries.name: Clíodhna
entries.note: dh is silent. The spelling Clíona is often said KLEE-nuh.

entries.name: Clodagh
entries.note: gh is silent.

entries.name: Colm
entries.note: Two syllables, not 'COLM'.

entries.name: Conchúr
entries.note: Irish form of Conor; pronunciation varies by region and some families simply say 'Conor', so check with the family. ch as in 'loch' is approximated with k.

entries.name: Dafydd
entries.note: dd = the 'th' in 'this'; English TTS voices the ending as the 'th' in 'thin'.

entries.name: Dáithí
entries.note: Irish form of David.

entries.name: Damilola
entries.note: Means 'bless me with wealth'. Often shortened to Dami.

entries.name: Darragh
entries.note: gh is silent.

entries.name: Dawit
entries.note: The Ethiopian and Eritrean form of David.

entries.name: Dearbhla
entries.note: bh = v; same name as Dervla.

entries.name: Deio
entries.note: Pet form of Dafydd. The final o is short, as in 'hop'. Welsh 'ei' sits between 'ay' and 'eye', so check with the family.

entries.name: Deniz
entries.note: Means 'sea'. Used for both boys and girls.

entries.name: Dev
entries.note: Means 'god'. Most UK families say DEV. In Hindi and Punjabi the vowel is longer, close to 'Dave'.

entries.name: Dhruv
entries.note: Means 'pole star'. The dh is a d with a puff of air, not the 'th' in 'this'.

entries.name: Diya
entries.note: Means 'lamp'.

entries.name: Dmytro
entries.note: The Ukrainian form of Dmitri. It starts with 'dm' (no vowel in between), and the stress is on the last syllable.

entries.name: Donnacha
entries.note: ch as in 'loch'; English TTS approximates it with k.

entries.name: Éabha
entries.note: Irish form of Eve; sounds like 'Ava' said the British way.

entries.name: Éadaoin
entries.note: Aideen is the usual English spelling of the same name.

entries.name: Éanna
entries.note: Traditionally a boy's name; now also used for girls.

entries.name: Ebuka
entries.note: Short for Chukwuebuka.

entries.name: Eesa
entries.note: The Arabic form of Jesus. The Isa spelling is still said with 'ee', not 'eye'.

entries.name: Efa
entries.note: Welsh f = v.

entries.name: Eilidh
entries.note: dh is silent.

entries.name: Eimear
entries.note: Irish speakers pronounce the final r (EE-mer).

entries.name: Eira
entries.note: Means 'snow'. Welsh 'ei' sits between 'ay' and 'eye', so families say it both ways.

entries.name: Eitan
entries.note: The Hebrew form of Ethan.

entries.name: Eleni
entries.note: The Greek form of Helen.

entries.name: Elif
entries.note: The stress is on the second syllable.

entries.name: Élodie
entries.note: Most UK families say EL-uh-dee; French families say ay-lo-DEE.

entries.name: Elowen
entries.note: Cornish for 'elm tree'. Cornish stresses the middle syllable: el-OH-wen.

entries.name: Emilia
entries.note: Italian, Spanish and Polish families usually say i-MEE-lee-uh.

entries.name: Emir
entries.note: Means 'prince' or 'commander'.

entries.name: Eoghan
entries.note: Irish families say it like Owen (the same sound as Eoin). Many Scottish families say YOH-uhn, closer to the Gaelic Eòghann.

entries.name: Eoin
entries.note: Sounds the same as Owen.

entries.name: Esmé
entries.note: Most UK families say EZ-mee; some keep the French ez-MAY.

entries.name: Evelyn
entries.note: For girls almost always EV-uh-lin; the older male form was EEV-lin.

entries.name: Evie
entries.note: Rhymes with 'Stevie', not 'Chevy'.

entries.name: Fearghal
entries.note: gh sounds like g; same name as Fergal.

entries.name: Fiachra
entries.note: ch as in 'loch'; English TTS approximates it with k.

entries.name: Fiadh
entries.note: dh is silent.

entries.name: Fionn
entries.note: Irish families often use the Irish vowel (FYUUN); otherwise it sounds like Finn.

entries.name: Fionnuala
entries.note: Often shortened to Nuala. The spelling Finola is usually said fin-OH-luh.

entries.name: Folake
entries.note: Means 'pampered with wealth'. It ends in a short 'keh'. In English it often drifts towards 'kay'.

entries.name: Freja
entries.note: The j sounds like y. Danish families say FRY-uh.

entries.name: Genevieve
entries.note: French families may say zhuhn-VYEV.

entries.name: Giovanni
entries.note: The i after G is silent: joh-VAH-nee.

entries.name: Giulia
entries.note: Italian form of Julia; the i after G is silent.

entries.name: Gonçalo
entries.note: The ç sounds like s.

entries.name: Grá
entries.note: Irish word for 'love'.

entries.name: Gruffudd
entries.note: dd = the 'th' in 'this'; English TTS voices it as in 'thin'.

entries.name: Guadalupe
entries.note: Often shortened to Lupe (LOO-pay).

entries.name: Guillermo
entries.note: The G is hard and the u is silent: gee-YAIR-moh.

entries.name: Gurleen
entries.note: The first syllable sounds like 'gur' in 'gurdwara'. In Punjabi it is shorter, with the u of 'put' and a lightly tapped r.

entries.name: Guto
entries.note: Pet form of Gruffudd. The u sounds like the i in 'sit', and the final o is short, as in 'hop' rather than 'hope'.

entries.name: Gwenllian
entries.note: Welsh ll is a breathy 'hl' sound that English TTS cannot make; approximated with l.

entries.name: Gwilym
entries.note: Welsh form of William.

entries.name: Ha-eun
entries.note: The eu is a short 'uh' with unrounded lips. It is not 'you' or 'oo'.

entries.name: Hamish
entries.note: Scottish form of James.

entries.name: Haoran
entries.note: Hao rhymes with 'now'.

entries.name: Harjot
entries.note: Means 'God's light'. The first syllable sounds like 'her'.

entries.name: Haruto
entries.note: Japanese uses pitch rather than stress, so the syllables are fairly even. The r is a light tap.

entries.name: Heledd
entries.note: dd = the 'th' in 'this'; English TTS voices it as in 'thin'.

entries.name: Hermione
entries.note: Four syllables.

entries.name: Hinata
entries.note: Means 'sunny place'. Used for both girls and boys.

entries.name: Hugh
entries.note: Sounds like 'hue'. The Welsh form Huw is said the same way.

entries.name: Hugo
entries.note: Spanish families drop the h: OO-goh. Portuguese families drop it too and end with an oo sound.

entries.name: Huong
entries.note: Means 'fragrance'. Said as one gliding syllable: the 'oo' is made with spread (unrounded) lips, and the ending is 'ung' as in 'lung'.

entries.name: Huw
entries.note: Welsh form of Hugh and said the same way. In Welsh the vowel glides from 'i' to 'oo'.

entries.name: Hywel
entries.note: Some English speakers say HOW-el.

entries.name: Iain
entries.note: Not 'EYE-an'.

entries.name: Ibrahim
entries.note: The Arabic form of Abraham. Some families put the stress at the start instead (IB-ruh-heem).

entries.name: Idris
entries.note: The Welsh name and many UK families say ID-ris. Many Arabic- and Urdu-speaking families say id-REES (also spelt Idrees).

entries.name: Ifan
entries.note: Welsh form of Evan (John). Welsh f = v, and the i is a long 'ee'.

entries.name: Ife
entries.note: Means 'love' in Yoruba, where it ends in a short 'eh', not 'ay'. As a short form of Igbo names such as Ifeoma it is EE-fay.

entries.name: Ifeoma
entries.note: Means 'good thing'. In Igbo the o is open, like the o in 'hot'; many people say ee-fay-OH-mah in English.

entries.name: Ignacio
entries.note: Families from Spain say ig-NAH-thee-oh.

entries.name: Ilhan
entries.note: A girls' name in Somali families, a boys' name in Turkish families.

entries.name: Imani
entries.note: Means 'faith'.

entries.name: Inaya
entries.note: Means 'care' or 'concern'.

entries.name: Inès
entries.note: The final s is pronounced. Portuguese families (usually spelt Inês) end it with a sh sound.

entries.name: Ioan
entries.note: Welsh form of John. Two syllables; the second vowel is a full 'a', not 'uh'.

entries.name: Ioana
entries.note: The Romanian form of Joanna.

entries.name: Iona
entries.note: After the island of Iona.

entries.name: Ishaan
entries.note: The stress is on the long 'ahn'.

entries.name: Ishbel
entries.note: Scottish form of Isobel.

entries.name: Isla
entries.note: s is silent in the usual pronunciation, as in 'island'.

entries.name: Iwan
entries.note: Welsh form of John. Welsh families say EE-wan (as the actor Iwan Rheon does); some English speakers say it like Ewan.

entries.name: Jabari
entries.note: Means 'brave'.

entries.name: Jago
entries.note: Cornish form of James.

entries.name: Jaime
entries.note: In the UK this spelling is usually said like Jamie. As a Spanish boys' name it is KHY-may, with a throaty h.

entries.name: Jakub
entries.note: The Polish form of Jacob. The j is said 'y' and the final b sounds like p.

entries.name: Jaspreet
entries.note: The first a sounds like the u in 'just', not the a in 'jazz'.

entries.name: Javier
entries.note: The J is a throaty h.

entries.name: Ji-woo
entries.note: Used for both girls and boys. In Korean it is two light, even syllables, jee + oo, with no real w sound.

entries.name: João
entries.note: The ending is a nasal 'ow' with no full n; the J is soft like the s in 'measure'.

entries.name: Joaquín
entries.note: The J is a throaty h (as in Scottish 'loch'), not a J sound.

entries.name: Joep
entries.note: The J sounds like y; rhymes with 'hoop'.

entries.name: Johann
entries.note: The J sounds like y.

entries.name: José
entries.note: Spanish families say khoh-SAY (the J is a throaty h, as in 'loch'); Portuguese families say zhoo-ZEH.

entries.name: Juan
entries.note: One syllable; the J is a throaty h.

entries.name: Jun
entries.note: Not said like the English 'Jun' in 'jungle'. In Mandarin the vowel is between 'oo' and 'ee'.

entries.name: Jürgen
entries.note: The J sounds like y.

entries.name: Kacper
entries.note: The Polish form of Casper. c is said 'ts', and in Polish the final r is lightly rolled.

entries.name: Kai
entries.note: Rhymes with 'sky'. The Welsh spelling Cai is said the same way.

entries.name: Kajus
entries.note: Lithuanian j = y.

entries.name: Karthik
entries.note: In Indian languages the th is a soft t, not the 'th' in 'thin'.

entries.name: Kavya
entries.note: Means 'poetry'.

entries.name: Kelechi
entries.note: Means 'praise God'.

entries.name: Kerensa
entries.note: Means 'love' in Cornish. Some families say kuh-REN-suh.

entries.name: Khadija
entries.note: In Arabic the kh is a soft throaty sound, as in 'loch'. Many UK families use a plain k.

entries.name: Kofi
entries.note: The Akan day name for a boy born on a Friday.

entries.name: Kojo
entries.note: The Akan day name for a boy born on a Monday.

entries.name: Krish
entries.note: Short for Krishna.

entries.name: Krzysztof
entries.note: The Polish form of Christopher. rz and sz both sound like 'sh' here, so there's no vowel between the k and the sh.

entries.name: Kwabena
entries.note: Akan day name for a boy born on a Tuesday.

entries.name: Kwame
entries.note: The Akan day name for a boy born on a Saturday.

entries.name: Lachlan
entries.note: Scottish families use the throaty 'ch' of 'loch' (LAKH-luhn); plain text-to-speech can only approximate it with a k. Most families in England say LAK-luhn; some say LOK-luhn, as Australians do.

entries.name: Layla
entries.note: Means 'night'. Some Arabic-speaking families say LYE-luh.

entries.name: Leah
entries.note: Most UK families say LEE-uh; some say LAY-uh, which is also the usual Leia pronunciation.

entries.name: Linh
entries.note: The final h is silent. Southern speakers say it closer to LIN.

entries.name: Llew
entries.note: Means 'lion'. Welsh ll is a breathy 'hl' sound that English TTS cannot make, so the Welsh variant is approximated with l. The 'ew' is one gliding syllable: eh-oo.

entries.name: Llinos
entries.note: Welsh ll is a breathy 'hl' sound that English TTS cannot make; approximated with l.

entries.name: Louis
entries.note: The s is usually silent in the UK (like Louie); some families say LOO-is.

entries.name: Lowenna
entries.note: Means 'joy'.

entries.name: Lowri
entries.note: LOW as in 'now'.

entries.name: Lucia
entries.note: Italian families say loo-CHEE-uh; families from Spain (usually spelt Lucía) say loo-THEE-uh.

entries.name: Łucja
entries.note: The Polish form of Lucy. ł is said like 'w' and c like 'ts'.

entries.name: Luis
entries.note: Portuguese families (Luís) often end it with a sh sound.

entries.name: Mairéad
entries.note: Irish form of Margaret. Scottish Gaelic speakers may say it differently.

entries.name: Maja
entries.note: In Polish, j is said like 'y'.

entries.name: Mali
entries.note: Not 'MAH-lee'.

entries.name: Manpreet
entries.note: In Punjabi the first a sounds like the u in 'fun', not the a in 'man'.

entries.name: Margot
entries.note: The final t (or x) is silent.

entries.name: Maryam
entries.note: The Arabic form of Mary. MARR sounds like the start of 'marry'. Many Pakistani families say MURR-yuhm.

entries.name: Matas
entries.note: Lithuanian form of Matthew.

entries.name: Matei
entries.note: Romanian form of Matthew.

entries.name: Méabh
entries.note: Rhymes with 'wave'.

entries.name: Mei
entries.note: Means 'beautiful'.

entries.name: Menzies
entries.note: Rare as a first name. The traditional Scottish form is MING-is; the z was once a different letter.

entries.name: Mhairi
entries.note: Mh = v.

entries.name: Micheál
entries.note: Irish form of Michael. Without the accent, Micheal is often just a spelling of Michael, so check with the family.

entries.name: Mihai
entries.note: The Romanian form of Michael.

entries.name: Mikołaj
entries.note: The Polish form of Nicholas. ł is said like 'w' and the final aj rhymes with 'why'.

entries.name: Min-jun
entries.note: Korean has no strong stress, so both syllables are fairly even.

entries.name: Minh
entries.note: The final h is silent.

entries.name: Mohammed
entries.note: Another spelling of Muhammad. Families who use this spelling usually start it with 'moh'; some say it exactly like Muhammad.

entries.name: Muhammad
entries.note: One of the most popular boys' names in the UK. In Arabic the m in the middle is doubled.

entries.name: Muireann
entries.note: Many speakers add a slight w after the M (MWIRR-uhn).

entries.name: Musa
entries.note: The Arabic form of Moses.

entries.name: Nacho
entries.note: Short for Ignacio.

entries.name: Nana
entries.note: Also an Akan title of respect. Used for both boys and girls. Not said like 'nanna' (grandma).

entries.name: Naoise
entries.note: Used for boys and girls.

entries.name: Nevaeh
entries.note: 'Heaven' spelt backwards.

entries.name: Ngozi
entries.note: Means 'blessing'. It starts with a short hummed 'n' (shown as 'uhn'). Keep it light, not 'en'.

entries.name: Nguyen
entries.note: Usually a family name, not a first name. In Vietnamese it is one syllable starting with the 'ng' sound in 'singer': northern speakers say roughly ngwee-uhn, southern speakers ngwing.

entries.name: Niamh
entries.note: mh = v. Rhymes with 'Eve'. Some Irish speakers say it in two quick beats (NEE-uv).

entries.name: Nicola
entries.note: In the UK a girl's name (NIK-uh-luh); in Italy a boy's name (nee-KOH-luh).

entries.name: Niels
entries.note: Dutch families say NEELS; Danish families say NELS.

entries.name: Nikhil
entries.note: In Hindi the kh is a k with a puff of air, not the 'ch' of 'loch'. Hindi speakers may stress the second syllable a little more.

entries.name: Noa
entries.note: A girl's name in Hebrew. It sounds the same as Noah.

entries.name: Noel
entries.note: British families usually say NOH-uhl; French-style noh-EL is also used, especially for girls (Noëlle).

entries.name: Noor
entries.note: Means 'light'. One syllable with a long 'oo', like 'poor' said with a long oo, not like 'door'. In Arabic and Urdu the final r is lightly rolled.

entries.name: Obinna
entries.note: Means 'father's heart'.

entries.name: Odhrán
entries.note: dh is silent.

entries.name: Oisín
entries.note: Never 'OY-sin'.

entries.name: Oleksandr
entries.note: The Ukrainian form of Alexander.

entries.name: Olena
entries.note: The Ukrainian form of Helen.

entries.name: Oliwia
entries.note: The Polish form of Olivia. w is said like 'v'.

entries.name: Oluwaseun
entries.note: Means 'thank you, God'. The s is said 'sh'. Often shortened to Seun (SHAY-oon).

entries.name: Oluwatobi
entries.note: Means 'God is great'. Often shortened to Tobi.

entries.name: Omar
entries.note: In Arabic this is the same name as Umar, and some Arabic-speaking families say OO-mar.

entries.name: Orlaith
entries.note: th is silent.

entries.name: Ottilie
entries.note: Most UK families stress the first syllable; some say o-TIL-ee. The German original is closer to o-TEE-lee-uh.

entries.name: Pádraig
entries.note: Irish form of Patrick.

entries.name: Penelope
entries.note: Four syllables, not 'PEN-uh-lohp'.

entries.name: Persephone
entries.note: Four syllables; the final e is pronounced.

entries.name: Piran
entries.note: Patron saint of Cornwall.

entries.name: Priya
entries.note: Means 'beloved'.

entries.name: Qing
entries.note: In pinyin, q is said like 'ch'.

entries.name: Rafe
entries.note: Old British form of Ralph; rhymes with 'safe'.

entries.name: Ralph
entries.note: Some traditional British families say RAYF (like Rafe).

entries.name: Ren
entries.note: Means 'lotus'. The r is a light tap.

entries.name: Rhodri
entries.note: Welsh rh is a breathy r; most families simply say ROD-ree.

entries.name: Rían
entries.note: Not 'Ryan'.

entries.name: Ríona
entries.note: Short for Ríonach. Some Irish speakers slip a slight 'uh' into the middle (REE-uh-nuh).

entries.name: Róisín
entries.note: Some families put more weight on the first syllable (ROH-sheen).

entries.name: Rowan
entries.note: In the second version ROW rhymes with 'now', as many Scots say the rowan tree.

entries.name: Ruairí
entries.note: Irish form of Rory; the first syllable is 'roo' not 'raw'.

entries.name: Ruaridh
entries.note: Scottish Gaelic form of Rory.

entries.name: Rutendo
entries.note: Means 'faith'.

entries.name: Saanvi
entries.note: Another name for the goddess Lakshmi.

entries.name: Sadhbh
entries.note: Rhymes with 'five'.

entries.name: Safa
entries.note: Means 'purity'. Also the name of a hill in Mecca. Some families stress the end: suh-FAH.

entries.name: Saoirse
entries.note: Means 'freedom'. Both forms are used in Ireland and the UK.

entries.name: Séamus
entries.note: Irish/Scottish form of James.

entries.name: Selam
entries.note: Means 'peace'.

entries.name: Senan
entries.note: The Irish spelling Seanán is said SHAN-awn.

entries.name: Senara
entries.note: Cornish saint of Zennor. Cornish names stress the second-to-last syllable.

entries.name: Seo-yeon
entries.note: In Korean, eo is an 'uh' sound made far back in the mouth, with the lips not rounded. It is not 'oh'.

entries.name: Seonaid
entries.note: Gaelic form of Janet.

entries.name: Seosamh
entries.note: Irish form of Joseph. mh = v in most of Ireland; in Ulster Irish the end sounds like 'oo'.

entries.name: Seren
entries.note: Means 'star'.

entries.name: Seun
entries.note: Short for Oluwaseun. The s is said 'sh'.

entries.name: Siân
entries.note: One syllable; not 'SEE-an'.

entries.name: Siddharth
entries.note: In Hindi the final th is a t with a puff of air, not the 'th' in 'thin'.

entries.name: Sigrid
entries.note: Norwegian families may say SEE-gree.

entries.name: Simran
entries.note: Means 'remembrance' or 'meditation'. Used for both girls and boys.

entries.name: Sìne
entries.note: Gaelic form of Jane.

entries.name: Siobhán
entries.note: bh = v; never 'see-OB-han'.

entries.name: Siôn
entries.note: Welsh John; one syllable, not 'SY-on'.

entries.name: Siu
entries.note: Said as one gliding syllable. It is the Cantonese form of Xiao.

entries.name: Sonny
entries.note: Sounds like 'sunny'.

entries.name: Sophia
entries.note: The traditional British suh-FY-uh is still used by some families.

entries.name: Sora
entries.note: Means 'sky'. The r is a light tap and the final a is a full 'ah'.

entries.name: Sorcha
entries.note: The Irish form has a 'ch' as in 'loch'; English TTS can only approximate it with k. Never 'SOR-shuh' or 'SOR-chuh'.

entries.name: St John
entries.note: As a first name it is traditionally said SIN-juhn.

entries.name: Ștefan
entries.note: In Romanian, ș is said 'sh'. English families usually say STEF-uhn.

entries.name: Szymon
entries.note: The Polish form of Simon. sz is said 'sh'.

entries.name: Tadhg
entries.note: dh is silent; rhymes with 'tiger' without the -er.

entries.name: Tamsin
entries.note: Some families say TAM-sin.

entries.name: Tatenda
entries.note: Means 'we are thankful'.

entries.name: Temi
entries.note: Means 'mine'. Often short for Temitope.

entries.name: Tendai
entries.note: Means 'be thankful'. Used for both boys and girls. English speakers often say TEN-dy instead.

entries.name: Thanh
entries.note: The th is a t with a puff of air, not the 'th' in 'thin'. Southern speakers say TAN; northern speakers say something closer to TYNG.

entries.name: Thea
entries.note: Scandinavian, Dutch and German families often say TAY-uh.

entries.name: Theo
entries.note: Dutch, German and Scandinavian families often say TAY-oh.

entries.name: Thomas
entries.note: The h is silent.

entries.name: Tiago
entries.note: Brazilian families say chee-AH-goo; families from Portugal say tee-AH-goo.

entries.name: Tobi
entries.note: Short for Oluwatobi. Sounds the same as Toby.

entries.name: Tolu
entries.note: Short for names like Toluwani and Toluwalase.

entries.name: Tomás
entries.note: Irish form of Thomas. Without the accent, Tomas is often a different (e.g. Lithuanian or Scandinavian) name.

entries.name: Ùisdean
entries.note: Gaelic form of Hugh.

entries.name: Veer
entries.note: Means 'brave'.

entries.name: Vihaan
entries.note: Means 'dawn'.

entries.name: Wiktoria
entries.note: In Polish, w is said like 'v'.

entries.name: Wojciech
entries.note: The final ch is a throaty sound, as in 'loch'.

entries.name: Xanthe
entries.note: X sounds like z; two syllables.

entries.name: Xavier
entries.note: Families differ: ZAY-vee-uh is most common in the UK; ig-ZAY-vee-uh is also widespread. French, Catalan and Portuguese families say it their own way.

entries.name: Xiao
entries.note: Said as one quick syllable: 'shee' slides straight into 'ow' (as in 'now'). Often part of a two-part name, like Xiaoming.

entries.name: Ximena
entries.note: The X is a throaty h (as in 'loch').

entries.name: Xin
entries.note: In pinyin, x is said like 'sh'.

entries.name: Xochitl
entries.note: The X sounds like s and the final tl is very light.

entries.name: Yael
entries.note: Two syllables, with the stress on the second.

entries.name: Yahya
entries.note: Arabic form of John. A soft breathy h ends the first syllable.

entries.name: Yasmin
entries.note: Means 'jasmine'.

entries.name: Yaw
entries.note: The Akan day name for a boy born on a Thursday. Ghanaian families say it to rhyme with 'now' (compare the Ivorian spelling Yao).

entries.name: Yiannis
entries.note: The Greek form of John.

entries.name: Yiming
entries.note: Mandarin uses tones instead of stress, so both syllables are fairly even.

entries.name: Yonas
entries.note: The Ethiopian and Eritrean form of Jonah.

entries.name: Yusuf
entries.note: The Arabic form of Joseph.

entries.name: Zakariya
entries.note: The Arabic form of Zachariah.

entries.name: Zayn
entries.note: Means 'beauty' or 'grace'. Sounds the same as the English name Zane.

entries.name: Zeynep
entries.note: The Turkish form of Zainab.

entries.name: Zhen
entries.note: The zh sounds close to English j, and the e is a short 'uh'.

entries.name: Zixuan
entries.note: The zi is a short buzzing 'dz'. The xuan sounds like 'shwen'.

entries.name: Zoe
entries.note: Two syllables.

entries.name: Zofia
entries.note: The Polish form of Sophia.

entries.name: Zuri
entries.note: Means 'beautiful'.

entries.name: Zuzanna
entries.note: The Polish form of Susanna.
